newsitem.title: FINLAND: INTERVIEW-Aamulehti cautious on ad growth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Aamulehti cautious on ad growth.

text.p: Finnish media group Aamulehti-Yhytyma is cautious about advertising growth despite sings that a recovery in the domestic economy is well under way and may accelerate, CEO Matti Packalen said on Thursday.
"I think people in the business are talking about how well things look but in the back of their heads, they still have warning signs," Packalen said in an interview with Reuters.
"Possibly things could turn to the better... but at the slightest jitter, people would hit the brakes," he said.
Finnish advertisers on Thursday released a 1997 barometer showing those expecting to increase advertising outnumbered those who expected to reduce it by a margin of 33 percentage points.

The comparable forecast a year ago showed a 63 percentage point margin despite a weaker domestic economic outlook then, so the barometer for next year reinforced his view that there is more cautiousness now, Packalen said.

According to Finnish Gallup-Mainostieto, last year's advertising growth was 12.5 percent with 10 percent growth in newspapers and freesheets. Newspapers and freesheets had a 59 percent stake and television 21 percent.
Packalen expected television's share to stabilise at about that level.

Aamulehti's operating profitability has improved this year. Its January-April operating income fell from 46 million markka but excluding a 13 million gain on a disposal in 1995, it rose eight million markka to 41 million, he noted.
And the group is on track to reach its 1.6 billion markka 1996 net sales forecast, up from 1.43 billion in 1995, he said.
"We are not worried about this year," he said.
Packalen declined to comment on this year's profit outlook, noting that the interim report will be published on October 9.
He said, however, that regional publisher Satakunnan Kirjateollisuus which Aamulehti bought in May -- expecting it may improve group profits already this year -- was a good buy.
"It looks so far to have been a good acquisition, there have been no surprises, at least nothing negative," he said.
Aamulehti paid 140 million markka for Satakunnan Kirjateollisuus which had 1995 net sales of over 193 million markka and posted a 16 million markka profit before extraordinary items.
Aamulehti's 1995 profit before extraordinary items rose to 87 million markka from 62 million. The January-April profit fell two million markka to 32 million this year.
It said in its January-April interim that it expected the full-year 1996 operating profit to improve on last year.

Packalen said Aamulehti targets an operating margin of 18 percent of turnover (16 percent in 1995), a 45 percent equity to assets ratio (43 percent at end-April) and a 15 percent return on investment (11.7 percent in 1995).
In the long run, Aamulehti looks for expansion in multimedia, but the whole sector of new media products is still very much looking for its future form, Packalen said.

Its involvement in two television projects with MTV3's Oy Kolmostelevisio Ab -- a local Helsinki channel called City-TV and a fourth national analogue channel -- will not bring fast money but a way to get a foothold in the future.
"In the channel 4 project, our intention is the get into the digital world. Our programmes are planned so that they could be directly transferred to a digital infrastructure," he said.
Aamulehti's joint venture channel intends to produce and broadcast programmes aimed at a youthful audience, focussing on sports and leisure. That would give a good segment, he said.
"Youth and leisure will always be there," he added.
Packalen expected the City-TV channel in Helsinki to become profitable in its third year, and a national channel to just break even in its fourth year.
The main return will not come until the age of digital television, he said.

But that may come sooner than some think. Packalen said he believed that the government might in the end decide against a fourth analogue TV channel concession and go straight for a few digital television channels instead. He hoped it would.
"Industrially it would make sense ... I'm sure the alternative is on the table too," he said.
He noted that Nokia -- one of Finnish industry's technological flagships -- manufactures signal converters which make regular television sets multimedia terminals.
"And Finns are testers. Finland is a very good testing ground for this kind of thing," he said, referring to the rapid spread of mobile telephones and the Internet in Finland.
For instance, Aamulehti has created Internet editions of its three main papers Aamulehti, Kauppalehti and Iltalehti and last year it started radio transmissions on the Net.
Aamulehti is now looking for ways to find out how people use the Net in order to guide product development, he said.
But he was confident newspapers would not die out.
"I believe the publisher of the future is a multifunction house, I don't think papers will disappear but other sorts of know-how is necessary too," he said.

Packalen was pleased by the fact that international investors, besides Aamulehti's main owner Swedish Marieberg , had increased their holdings in the group this year to 24 percent from 21 percent at the end of last year.
"It is good, they are very demanding," he said.

Of Aamulehti's market capitalisation, 60 percent is still traded on the illiquid and internationally little known Brokers' list and Packalen said there are no obstacles to introducing the vote-strong series I shares on the Helsinki Stock Exchange.
But there are no current plans for this, he said.
The two share series have not been traded since last Friday when both closed at 114 markka.

Marieberg has said it does not plan to increase its stake in Aamulehti since it reached 20 percent, which after conversion of bonds would give it the 25 percent of capital needed for it to consolidate profits.
